Recover
re-KUV-ur
v.t. and v.i. (to regain what was lost; to be restored from sickness; rendering Hebrew shub in the causative, nazal, Greek ananepho)
From Old French recovrer, Latin recuperare, to get back. The English preserves both senses Scripture uses — to regain a possession, and to return to health — and joins them to a third, the recovery of a man out of a snare.

Biblical Definition

To recover is to get back what was lost, and Scripture uses the word for territory, for health, and most importantly for men. David at Ziklag, having lost everything to the Amalekites, asks the Lord whether to pursue, and receives an unusually complete promise: “Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all” (1 Samuel 30:8). The passage is a study in the right order — David first encouraged himself in the LORD his God, then enquired, then pursued. Isaiah applies the word to the remnant, promising that the Lord “shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people” (Isaiah 11:11), a recovery from every direction of the compass that the New Testament sees fulfilled in the gathering of the elect from all nations. The most searching use is Paul's. Describing how a minister should deal with those who oppose themselves, he says correction is to be given in meekness, “if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth; And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will” (2 Timothy 2:25-26). The Greek ananepho means to become sober again, to come to oneself as a man does after drink — and the whole recovery is bracketed by God's giving of repentance on one side and the devil's captivity on the other. The man does return to his senses, and he could not have without the gift.

Webster 1828 Definition

To regain what was lost. David recovers all at Ziklag after enquiring of the LORD; Isaiah promises the recovery of the remnant; and Paul describes captives of the devil recovering themselves — coming to sobriety — when God gives repentance.

RECOVER, v.t. [Fr. recouvrer; L. recupero.] To regain; to get or obtain that which was lost; as, to recover stolen goods.

2. To restore from sickness; to heal; as, to recover one of a wound or disease.

3. To revive from apparent death; as, to recover a drowned person.

4. To regain by reparation or amends; as, to recover the time lost.

RECOVER, v.i. To grow well; to be restored from sickness or disorder; as, the patient recovered.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 2:26 — "And that they may recover themselves out of the snare of the devil, who are taken captive by him at his will."

1 Samuel 30:8 — "And David enquired at the LORD, saying, Shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? And he answered him, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all."

Isaiah 11:11 — "And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea."

2 Kings 5:3 — "And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy."

Modern Corruption

The reflexive recover themselves in 2 Timothy 2:26 is used to prove that fallen men have the native power to free themselves — a reading that severs the clause from the verse before it, where God gives the repentance.

expand to see more

The argument is simple and superficially strong: Paul says they may recover themselves, therefore the will is free and grace is resistible in the Arminian sense. The passage will not carry it. Paul's sentence begins in verse 25 with a condition entirely outside the man — if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth — and ends in verse 26 with a bondage entirely outside his control, taken captive by the devil at his will, the devil's will and not the captive's. Between those two clauses the man does indeed come to his senses and act; that is what regeneration produces, and the Reformed doctrine has never denied that the converted man genuinely wills, chooses, and repents. What it denies is that the willing is the cause rather than the effect. The verse teaches monergism and real human agency in one breath, which is precisely the confessional position.

There is a pastoral corruption on the other side worth naming, since ministers fall into it more often. Paul frames the whole recovery as a reason for gentleness: the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. A minister who holds the doctrine of divine sovereignty and uses it to justify harshness toward the erring has taken the theology and refused the tone the same sentence commands. God's freedom to grant repentance is the reason to keep instructing patiently, not a reason to stop.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shub in the hiphil (to bring back, restore) and 'asaph (to gather in, and so to heal of leprosy); Greek ananepho (to become sober again) and anablepsis (recovering of sight).

expand to see more

Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, return; in the causative, to bring back or recover; also the standard verb for repentance.

Hebrew 'asaph (H622) — to gather, take away; used in 2 Kings 5 of recovering Naaman of his leprosy.

Hebrew nazal, chayah (H2421) — to live, revive; used of recovery from sickness, as of Hezekiah in Isaiah 38:9.

Greek ananepho (G366) — to return to soberness, come to one's senses; the vivid hapax of 2 Timothy 2:26.

Greek anablepsis (G309) — recovering of sight; the noun in Luke 4:18, quoted from Isaiah 61.

Usage

"“Without fail recover all” — given to David after he encouraged himself in the LORD and enquired."

"“Recover themselves out of the snare of the devil” — genuine human action, produced by repentance God gives."

"“Recover the remnant of his people” — the gathering of the elect from every quarter."
